lead: Today's readings are about how the word of God is received. Paul thanks God that the Thessalonians accepted his preaching “not as a human word but as what it really is, God's word”, and he knows what it cost them. In the Gospel many disciples have turned away after the teaching on the bread of life, and Peter answers for the Twelve: “Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.” The key words are receive and believe.

r.h: Not as a human word but as God's word
set: 1 Thessalonians is very probably the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent by Paul from Corinth around AD 50–51. Acts tells how Paul preached in the synagogue of Thessalonica, how some Jews and many Greeks believed, and how opposition forced him to leave by night (Acts 17:1–10). The young church had suffered from the start.

Verses 14–16 contain the sharpest words Paul ever wrote about some of his own people. They must be read with care. Paul was himself a Jew, proud of his people and grieving for them (Romans 9:1–5; 11:1). Here he speaks of particular opponents in Judea who had persecuted the churches there and tried to stop the preaching to the Gentiles, just as the Thessalonians suffered from “your own compatriots”. A few scholars have thought these verses were added later, but most accept them as Paul's. Either way, the Church reads them in the light of his mature teaching in Romans 9–11.
str: v. 13: thanksgiving: the word received as God's word, at work in believers.
v. 14: the Thessalonians share the sufferings of the churches in Judea.
vv. 15–16: Paul's complaint against those who opposed the Gospel and hindered his mission.
kw: Two verbs. The first is the word for receiving a tradition handed on, used of the Lord's Supper and of the Resurrection (1 Corinthians 11:23; 15:3). The second means to welcome a guest. The Thessalonians did both: they took in the teaching and made it at home in their hearts.
From this verb comes our word “energy”. God's word is not a dead letter. It goes on working in those who believe.
The Thessalonians did not set out to imitate anyone's sufferings. They found themselves walking the same road as the first churches, and so they became, in Paul's eyes, part of one family.
vv: you accepted it not as a human word but as what it really is, God’s word, which is also at work in you believers.
Paul does not deny that he spoke with a human voice. He says that through his human words God himself was speaking. This is how the Church understands all preaching that is faithful to the apostles.
For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the churches of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea,
The first Christians in Judea were themselves Jews. Paul's comparison is between persecuted believers in two places, not between two peoples.
by hindering us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved.
This is the heart of Paul's complaint: not who these opponents were, but that they tried to block the Gospel. Scholars do not agree what event Paul means by the “wrath” at the end of the verse.
ch: The Catechism takes up verse 13 to describe how the Church receives Scripture: she welcomes it not as a human word but as what it really is, the word of God, and finds in it her nourishment and her strength (CCC 104). On verses 14–16 the Church is clear. The Second Vatican Council teaches that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today, and that the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Paul himself writes later that “God has not rejected his people” (Romans 11:1–2) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).

r.h: Lord, to whom can we go?
set: These verses close the long sixth chapter of John. Jesus has fed the five thousand and then, in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59), has spoken of himself as the bread of life and of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples say, “This teaching is difficult” (6:60), and many turn back (6:66). This is the first time John names “the twelve”. John has no scene at Caesarea Philippi; this is his form of Peter's confession.
str: v. 67: Jesus' question to the Twelve.
v. 68: Peter's answer: there is no one else to go to.
kw: Peter repeats what Jesus has just said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (6:63). The words that drove others away are the very words Peter cannot leave.
we have come to believe and know
Both verbs are in a tense that speaks of a settled state: we have believed and we still believe; we have come to know and we still know. Faith comes first, and knowledge grows from it.
A rare title. In the other Gospels it is spoken by an unclean spirit (Mark 1:24; Luke 4:34). Here it is spoken by a disciple in faith. Jesus is the one whom the Father has set apart and sent (10:36).
vv: Do you also wish to go away?
Jesus does not soften his teaching to keep the Twelve. He respects their freedom, and the question is a real one.
Lord, to whom can we go? You have the words of eternal life.
Peter does not say that he understands everything. He has looked at every other road and found none that leads to life.
We have come to believe and know that you are the Holy One of God.
Some later manuscripts read “the Christ, the Son of the living God”, the wording of Matthew 16:16. The best manuscripts have the shorter and more unusual title, which the NRSV follows.
ch: The Catechism says that the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the Passion scandalized them, and that the question “Do you also wish to go away?” goes on through the ages, inviting us to discover that only the Lord has the words of eternal life (CCC 1336). St Augustine noted that Peter says “we have come to believe and know”, not the other way round: we believe in order to understand (Tractates on John 27, in substance). That is the faith we bring to the Holy Qurbono: we do not see how the bread becomes his Body, but we believe his word.

qa: Does Paul blame the Jewish people for the death of Jesus?

No. Paul, a Jew himself, complains of particular opponents of his day who persecuted believers and hindered his mission. The Church teaches that the passion of Christ cannot be charged against all Jews of that time or of today, and that all sinners were the authors of his sufferings (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597–598). Paul's own last word on his people is hope: “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26).
rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Philip Neri (1515–1595), a priest of Rome born in Florence. He founded the Congregation of the Oratory, where people met to pray, to hear the word of God explained simply, and to sing. He was known for his joy and his humour, for long hours in the confessional, and for his love of the Holy Eucharist. He shows what Peter's answer looks like in a life: a man who had found the words of eternal life and could not stop sharing them.
study: When a teaching of the Church seems hard to me, do I walk away, or do I say with Peter, “Lord, to whom can we go?”
How do I listen to the readings in the Holy Qurbono: as a human word, or as God's word at work in me?
